title: Combined effects of acoustic, thermal, and illumination conditions on the comfort of discrete senses and overall indoor environment
research_question: To investigate the influence of multisensory interaction on acoustic comfort, thermal comfort, visual comfort, and indoor environmental comfort with three physical indoor environmental factors (acoustic, thermal, and illumination conditions) in an environmentally controlled laboratory.

participants.description: 60 university students (30 men, 30 women) with normal hearing (0-25 dB HL) and normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no color deficiency. Wore a clothing ensemble of approximately 0.75 clo.
participants.recruitment: Received financial support for their participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four different sound sources (babble, fan, music, water) played at four sound levels (45, 55, 65, 75 dBA). Ambient noise level in the laboratory was 35 dBA. Each sound stimulus was presented for 25 s.
Three homogeneous room temperatures (20, 25, 30 °C) corresponding to cool, neutral, and warm sensations, with a constant relative humidity of 45%. Local air velocity was less than 0.1 m/s.
Three illuminance levels on the participants' desk surface (150, 500, 1000 lx). The color temperature of the fluorescent lamp was 6500 K.

mechanisms: Humans perceive environments through the interaction and integration among various sensory stimuli, leading to multisensory interaction effects on comfort perception.

Specific physical indoor environmental factors have the greatest effect on their corresponding sensory comfort, but other physical factors also affect the perception of subjective comfort through cross-modal interactions.
implementation_implications: Acoustic design should be prioritized as acoustic factors had the greatest impact on overall indoor environmental comfort among the tested factors.
Gender differences should be considered in the design of indoor environments, as gender moderates comfort perceptions across various physical conditions.

limitations: The experimental design, with time-varying sound stimuli and steady-state thermal/illumination, might have caused participants to focus more on acoustic variations, potentially limiting the generalizability of thermal/illumination effects.
Illuminance was the sole physical factor for visual comfort; other visual factors (e.g., color temperature of lighting, wall color, window views) were not studied.
Gender differences in comfort perception cannot be generalized without considering specific environmental conditions, as effects varied across conditions.
